In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the molecular defects in patients with isolated complex I deficiency and their consequences on the integrity of the respiratory chain.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of mitochondrial diseases, with the aim of developing a better diagnostic and prognostic strategy and of identifying potential therapeutic targets.
the elucidation of the pathogenesis of complex I deficiency, which will help us to understand better the clinical manifestations of this disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the assembly of mitochondrial OXPSHOS complexes can be impaired by nuclear-encoded complex I mutations, with different effects on the integrity of other OXPHOS components.
complex I mutations affect the stability and/or assembly of the complex itself, but also of other OXPHOS components.
complex I assembly defects are the most frequent cause of isolated complex deficiency, whereas catalytic defects are more frequently found in patients with combined OXPHOS deficiencies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the assembly of complex I is affected in patients with mutations on structural subunits, while mutations in genes encoding for catalytic subunits lead to a decrease in the enzymatic activity without affecting assembly of complex I.

mutations in nuclear-encoded genes for the complex I subunits affect the integrity and stability of the complex, and that the assembly of the peripheral arm of the complex I is particularly affected in these mutations.
the integrity of mitochondrial complexes is affected in patients harboring different types of nuclear mutations in complex I genes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the analysis of the integrity of mitochondrial complexes by BN-PAGE can provide important information on the pathogenic mechanism of complex I deficiencies.
complex I assembly defects can be identified by a specific pattern of complex I subcomplexes and a decrease in the levels and activity of intact complex I.

mutations in different nuclear genes can affect the assembly and/or stability of complex I in a different manner, and that the analysis of the levels of fully-assembled OXPHOS supercomplexes is a useful tool for understanding the pathogenesis of complex I deficiency.
